subtitulo_topo: The waiting list for speech therapy in Brazil's SUS

visual.alt: Winding line of 393 dots, each one representing a person who was waiting for speech therapy and agreed to take part in the research.

passos.texto: The waiting list for speech therapy in Brazil's public health system (SUS), in a municipality in the interior of São Paulo state: who was waiting, what they needed and what changed after a phone call.
passos.extra: Study by Salles, Santos, Moraes, Alpes and Ferreira-Vasques · CoDAS, 2026

link.rotulo: Prefer to read it as text? Open the study page →

passos.texto: Each dot is one person. There are 393: the people who answered the phone and agreed to take part in the research.
They were referred by primary health units between February 2018 and December 2022. Some had been waiting for about five years.

itens.desc: muscles of the mouth and face

cenas.alt: Six simple drawings of the areas of speech-language pathology: language, voice, audiology, dysphagia, orofacial myology and otoneurology.

passos.texto: It deals with human communication: language, speech, voice, hearing and functions of the mouth and face, such as chewing and swallowing.
In the study, each person on the list was assigned the subarea able to address their complaint. Language and dysphagia were split into child and adult.
In the SUS, speech therapists work from the primary health unit to the hospital. To plan this care, it is necessary to know who is waiting and what they need.

faixas.rotulo: Referrals that made up the list

cenas.alt: Timeline: referrals from February 2018 to December 2022 and phone calls from July 2023 to July 2024.

passos.texto: The list gathered referrals made from February 2018 to December 2022.
The research called these people from July 2023 to July 2024.
Staying on the list for a long time, with no care or guidance, can make the condition worse and lead people to give up on the care they need.

itens.texto: It was held by CREDAC, the center that allocates the municipality's appointments. The staff in charge of it were not speech therapists.
Sex, age, initial complaint, current complaint and the subarea able to help.
Trained students called, invited people and sent the consent form. For minors, they spoke with a parent or guardian.
Keep waiting, leave the list or schedule an appointment.

cenas.alt: Four steps: the list at CREDAC, the spreadsheet, the phone call and the decision about each person.

passos.titulo: A phone call for each person
passos.texto: Speech therapy students, supervised by professors, carried out the research as a final undergraduate project and a university outreach project.
In each call, they updated the person's details and indicated the speech therapy subarea that matched the current complaint.
Finally, they decided what to do with each case. People with no phone or who did not live in the municipality were left out.
passos.ausente: how many people were on the list in total and how many could not be reached.

passos.titulo: Who was still on the list
passos.texto: 418 people were contacted.
393 agreed to take part; the other 25 did not.
36 had already been treated at another service, public or private.
In 70, the complaint had resolved on its own.
41 had moved to another city, state or country. That left 246 people who still needed care.

visual.nota: In the article's flowchart (Figure 1), those scheduled appear as 66.9%; by the counts in the text, 162 out of 246 is 65.9%, as in the abstract.

cenas.alt: Two rows of dots: 162 people scheduled and 84 who kept waiting.

passos.titulo: What changed after the phone call
passos.texto: With the complaint analyzed and the subarea assigned, 162 of the 246 people were scheduled for care.
84 kept waiting for an appointment.

visual.nota: Ages from 1 year and 9 months to 81 years and 1 month.

cenas.alt: Four rows of dots: 177 children, 35 adolescents, 20 young adults and middle-aged people and 14 older people.

passos.texto: Of the 246 people, 177 were children up to 11 years old: 71.9% of the list.
There were also 35 adolescents, 20 young adults and middle-aged people and 14 older people.
158 were male (64.2%). The authors link this to the higher occurrence of neurodevelopmental delays in this group, according to the literature.

itens.texto: kept the complaint on the referral form (73.2%).
had a complaint different from the referral (26.8%).
itens.cuidado: Some cases had gotten worse during the wait, according to the authors.

cenas.alt: Two numbers: 180 people kept the complaint on the referral and 66 had a different complaint.

passos.texto: For 1 in 4 people, the current complaint was different from the one on the referral.
With a long wait, records become outdated and needs can change.

visual.titulo: People who needed a single subarea (217)
visual.eixo: Number of people, according to the text of the Results.
visual.alt: Bars: child language 182, adult language 9, adult dysphagia 7, voice 5, audiology 4, child dysphagia 4, orofacial myology 3 and otoneurology 3.

passos.texto: 217 people needed a single subarea. For 182 of them, it was child language.
Next came adult language, adult dysphagia and voice. Audiology, child dysphagia, orofacial myology and otoneurology had 3 or 4 people each.
Most referrals, made by primary care physicians, were for child language, as in other Brazilian studies.

visual.titulo: People who needed two or three subareas (29)
visual.eixo: Number of people, from Table 1 (percentages of 29).
visual.alt: Bars: audiology and child language 16, dysphagia and adult language 5, dysphagia and child language 2, child language and orofacial myology 2, and 4 other combinations with 1 person each.

passos.texto: 29 people needed two or three subareas. The most common combination was audiology with child language: 16.
For the authors, these cases show the importance of broad, generalist training that looks at the whole person.
Even so, referrals to a single subarea predominated, which, according to the authors, reveals limits in understanding what speech therapists do.

linhas.a: 393 people who agreed to take part

cenas.alt: Table comparing the list before and after the phone calls.

passos.texto: Of the 393 people who took part, 84 were still waiting at the end of the action.
For the authors, having the speech therapist involved in allocating appointments, or guiding those who do it, made scheduling more accurate.
They argue that the waiting list should be seen as an indicator of access and equity, not just as a working tool.

itens.texto: Train primary care professionals to make more detailed referrals.

itens.titulo: Speech therapists in primary health units
itens.texto: Having a speech therapist in primary health units.
They can reduce the effects of delays in diagnosis or intervention.
With in-person reception and joint discussions with health teams (matrix support).

passos.texto: To avoid such long lists, the authors suggest acting before the list grows.
And they call for the study to continue, to better understand who is waiting for care in the public sector.

itens.texto: The results cannot be generalized to other cities.
The list's data had incomplete and outdated information.
People without a phone or with a disconnected number were left out.
The analysis was descriptive only, with totals and percentages.

itens.titulo: Information the article does not provide
itens.texto: How many people were on the list in total and how long, on average, each one waited.

cenas.alt: List of the study's limitations and of information the article does not provide.

passos.titulo: What the study does not show
passos.texto: The authors themselves point out the limits of the research.
Because it was done by phone only, the research did not reach people who had no contact.
And there are numbers the article does not report.

visual.titulo: The same 393 people, after the action
visual.alt: The same line of 393 dots, now in color: 162 scheduled, 84 waiting and 147 who left the list.

passos.texto: A phone call turned an old list into information: who still needed care, what for, and who could be seen.
Of the 393 people, 162 were scheduled, 84 kept waiting and 147 left the list.
For the authors, organizing the list is not only a task for management: it is also a challenge for health professionals, especially speech therapists.
